Good question — the right Windsurf model depends on the kinds of work you’ll hand off. I don’t have Windsurf’s exact model names, so below I’ll give a practical decision framework, a mapping from task → model type, and a short, repeatable test you can run to pick the best model from the ones Windsurf shows you. Paste the model names you see in Windsurf and I’ll recommend a specific one.

1) Quick decision rules
- If you want fast, low-cost edits (small UI tweaks, single-file fixes): choose a smaller, faster code model (low latency).
- If you need multi‑file changes, architecture refactors, or reasoning about app state and lifecycles (playback lifecycle, Supabase integration): pick a larger code-specialized model with a big context window.
- If you want tests, docs, or careful refactors with minimal regressions: use a code-specialized model that’s optimized for synthesis + tests.
- If you expect the AI to run tools (git, build, tests) or integrate with your repo view, prefer a model that supports tool use / persistent project context.

2) Matching model capabilities to tasks
- Small, deterministic edits (styling, import fixes, small bug): small/medium code model; set temperature low (0–0.2).
- Multi-file refactor or feature (teaser marks wiring, playback lifecycle change): large code model with full-repo context.
- Generate tests, CI, or migration scripts: medium-to-large model with an emphasis on correctness and code-quality.
- Exploratory design or multiple options (UI variations): medium model with higher temperature (0.3–0.6) to get diverse ideas.

3) Recommended runtime settings (for code work)
- Temperature: 0–0.2 for deterministic code; up to 0.4 for creative UI variants.
- Max tokens / context window: use the largest context available for repo-scale tasks so the model can see multiple files.
- Few-shot: include 1–2 examples of desired output format (patch, PR description, tests).
- Output format: request unified diff or explicit file patch blocks so you can apply changes automatically.

4) Quick 3-step evaluation to run on 2–3 candidate models
Try this same set of small-but-representative tasks on each model and compare outputs.

Setup: pick 2–3 candidate models from Windsurf.

Task A (small): Fix SongCard import style and whitespace (single-file).
- Prompt: “Apply only formatting and a single-line import change to SongCard.tsx: change `import React from 'react'` to `import * as React from 'react'`. Return a git-style patch for that file only.”

Task B (medium): Wire teaser-selection helper into PlaybackContext:
- Prompt: “Add a call to markTeaserIfNeeded(...) before loading a track in PlaybackContext.tsx so that playback uses teaser_url if present. Keep behavior backwards compatible. Return a patch covering only src/contexts/PlaybackContext.tsx and src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts if you modify it. Include brief explanation and tests or manual test steps.”

Task C (safety/reliability): Produce a unit test or manual test checklist ensuring playback unloads previous Audio.Sound before loading new one.

Evaluation metrics (score each model 1–5)
- Correctness: does generated code compile / run? (build + typecheck)
- Minimality: only changed intended files & lines
- Explanation: clear rationale and testing steps
- Regressions: did anything else break?
- Speed / cost: how fast & costly is the response

5) Practical recommendation (if you can’t run the test now)
- Start with a code-specialized larger model with the biggest context window Windsurf offers. Use low temperature and require patches + tests. That will maximize correctness and ability to reason over multiple files (teaser wiring is a multi-file consideration).
- For routine small PRs, switch to a cheaper/smaller code model to save credits.

6) Safety & workflow tips
- Always require the model to output a git patch or PR branch diff, not raw file replacements.
- Use your sanitized repo instance and a throwaway Supabase test project.
- Run CI / TypeScript compile and unit tests automatically on every AI PR before merge.
- Keep human code review mandatory for any AI-produced PR touching playback, auth, or secrets.

Next step from me
- Paste the list of Windsurf model names you see (or a screenshot/text) and I’ll map each to the guidance above and recommend one or two to try first — plus I’ll craft the exact prompts to run Tasks A/B/C for direct comparison. Which models are available in your Windsurf UI?

Purpose of this document
- Explain exactly where the project stands right now regarding “teaser” playback and “marks”.
- Describe the intent, data shapes, files involved, expected behavior, constraints, and open questions.
- This is a status/architecture brief only — no action requests.

Context snapshot
- App: React Native (Expo managed) + TypeScript
- Audio: expo-av (Audio.Sound)
- Backend: Supabase (client/anon access in dev)
- UI: Glass-styled components (GlassView, GlassDrawer), MiniPlayer overlay, SongCard list items
- Repo: sanitized working copy (no secrets), with helpers for “teaser marks” present but NOT fully wired into core playback

High-level: what “teaser marks” are meant to accomplish
- Allow certain songs to play a short preview (“teaser”) instead of (or before) the full track.
- The “mark” is metadata indicating that a song should use teaser playback and where to fetch it.
- Target behavior is reversible and feature-flagged: the system should be able to run with or without teaser mode.

Definitions
- Teaser: a short audio clip (e.g., 15–30 seconds) designated for preview.
- Mark: metadata that identifies a song as having a teaser (and provides its source).
  - Minimal mark fields: is_teaser: boolean, teaser_url: string (or a storage path resolvable to a public URL).
- Full track: the normal, complete audio source for a song (e.g., song.uri.uri).

Where the code stands right now
- PlaybackContext.tsx
  - Provides global playback state via React Context.
  - Manages a single Audio.Sound instance lifecycle (load → play; stop/unload on track change).
  - Song type in context currently focuses on full-track playback fields:
    - id: string | number
    - title: string
    - artist?: string | null
    - uri?: { uri: string } | undefined
    - cover_url?: string | null
  - Note: earlier experimental imports (markTeaserIfNeeded, useSupabaseClient) were removed from the tracked file to stabilize baseline. No teaser-specific logic is currently invoked here.
- Helpers present (but not fully integrated):
  - src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts — intended place to centralize teaser/mark decisions near playback context.
  - src/utils/marks.ts — generic mark utilities (e.g., normalize/check presence of teaser fields).
  - src/utils/actor.ts — scaffolding for future action/state-machine handling around playback decisions.
  - Hooks folder (src/hooks/) — where a useSupabaseClient or related integration may live for fetching/deriving marks.
- UI
  - HomeScreen.tsx renders the song list (source may be static or fetched).
  - SongCard.tsx displays each song; no explicit teaser badge/label wired right now.
  - MiniPlayerOverlay.tsx shows now-playing info; no teaser-specific display or restrictions yet.
- Config
  - app.json includes plugin "expo-font". No teaser config is in app.json (teaser should be controlled via code/env flag).

Intended data model (Supabase) — indicative (not prescriptive)
- songs table (example fields):
  - id (PK), title, artist, cover_url, full_uri (or storage path), created_at
  - teaser_url (nullable): direct URL or resolvable storage path for preview clip
  - is_teaser (boolean, derived or stored): if true, default playback should favor the teaser clip
- Policies:
  - Anon read allowed for public songs (RLS configured appropriately).
  - No service_role keys in the client.

Target behavior (teaser-first mode)
- Selection:
  - When a user taps a song, playback logic first checks for teaser marks (is_teaser or teaser_url).
- Source resolution:
  - If a valid teaser_url exists (or can be derived), load and play the teaser clip.
  - If no teaser is available, fall back to the full track (song.uri.uri).
- UI expectations (non-binding for now):
  - Optional “Preview” indicator on cards/mini player when teaser is playing.
  - If a teaser ends, playback stops (unless product decides to auto-continue — currently unspecified).
- Audio lifecycle constraints:
  - Never allow overlapping sounds; unload previous Audio.Sound before loading new source.
  - Handle load/play errors gracefully with logged context.

Non-goals (current phase)
- No in-app purchase or “unlock full track” flow is defined here.
- No automatic transition from teaser to full track is mandated at this stage.
- No new dependencies should be introduced solely for teaser logic.

Implementation approach (planned structure; helpers exist but wiring is pending)
- A pure function markTeaserIfNeeded(song) in playbackMarks.ts (or equivalent) should:
  - Inspect song + marks, return a resolved playback source object:
    - { uri: teaser_url } if teaser is applicable and available
    - otherwise the original full { uri }
  - Keep this logic isolated from UI components.
- The PlaybackContext will call that function before loading a track, deciding which source to feed into expo-av.
- utils/marks.ts will host small utilities:
  - hasTeaser(song): boolean
  - getTeaserUrl(song): string | null
  - normalizeSource(song): { uri: string }  // fallback handling
- Feature flag (environment or static flag):
  - TEASER_MODE=on|off (or a code-level flag) to quickly disable teaser behavior without invasive changes.

Edge cases to be mindful of (documented only)
- teaser_url is present but 403/404: treat as unavailable, fall back to full track.
- teaser_url is a storage path not a URL: must be resolvable to a public URL before play.
- Song without uri and without teaser_url: do not attempt play; surface an error state.
- Rapid song switching: ensure sound instance cleanup before new load to avoid “stuck” audio.

Quality expectations (descriptive)
- With teaser mode on, teaser-capable songs play previews reliably; without teaser, full tracks play.
- No duplicate or overlapping audio instances occur.
- Errors are surfaced in dev logs to aid debugging.

Open questions (for product/owner)
- Should teaser auto-advance into full track when available?
- What is the canonical duration for teaser clips (fixed vs. pre-cut asset)?
- Should UI display a distinct “Preview” badge, and where?
- Is teaser mode the default in production, or opt-in behind a flag?

Security and privacy
- No service_role or private keys in client.
- Only use Supabase anon key for public data in development.
- If signed URLs are required, generation must happen off-client (not part of this repo).

Summary
- The project is at a stable baseline with helpers for teaser/mark logic present but not wired into the core playback flow.
- PlaybackContext currently plays full tracks; teaser behavior is specified conceptually and the integration point is defined (a pre-load source selection step via a helper).
- UI does not yet indicate teaser status; any visuals are considered optional until product decisions are finalized.

(End of status — no requested actions in this document.)

Good question — pick the model that matches the work you want Windsurf to do. Short answer and recommendation up front, then the reasoning and exact practical guidance (which model(s) to use, when to switch, and an example first prompt + acceptance criteria you can paste into Windsurf.

Recommended pick (single primary model)
- Use the code-focused, large-capacity “Full‑Stack / Code” model (the biggest code-aware model Windsurf offers — often labelled something like “Code-Dev (Large)” or “Full-Stack AI”). 
  - Why: it has the best context window and reasoning for reading a repo, editing TypeScript/React Native code, wiring a context/hook, and producing safe backend integration notes for Supabase.

When to use specialty models (in addition)
- UI / design polish: use a “Frontend / React Native UI” specialist model for layout, animations, accessibility text, and snapshot-style UI changes.
- Database / SQL: use a “DB / SQL” or “Supabase specialist” model for schema/migration work, or converting storage paths to signed URLs and writing migration SQL.
- Security / secrets audits: use a security/audit model to check there are no leaked keys or dangerous patterns.
- Tests / QA: use a “Test Generator” model to produce unit tests and E2E steps (or a smaller faster model to iterate test cases).

Why this split
- The Full‑Stack code model is best for architectural changes, refactors, and cross-cutting edits (PlaybackContext + playbackMarks + hooks + Supabase wiring).
- Smaller or specialist models are faster/cheaper for focused tasks (UI tweaks, SQL).

Practical selection criteria for Windsurf models
- Must understand TypeScript and React Native (expo-av specifically is a plus).
- Must accept repo context or files upload and be able to edit multiple files and open PRs.
- Prefer larger context window if you’ll provide several files and README onboarding.
- Prefer a model that can generate tests and runnable commands (so you can verify locally).

How to run the workflow with minimal risk
1. Use the sanitized repo you already created (D:\coffee-native-windsurf). Tell Windsurf explicitly to work only in that repo/branch.
2. Give the onboarding files: README-windsurf-onboarding.md and docs/current-state-teaser-marks.md plus .env.example.
3. Ask Windsurf to create a feature branch for each task and open small PRs (one change per PR).
4. Require that no secrets or prod keys are added and that all Supabase access uses a throwaway test project or SQL schema only.

Exact initial task I recommend (what you should ask Windsurf to do first)
- Implement and wire the teaser selection so playback is feature-flagged and robust:
  - Create a pure function markTeaserIfNeeded(song, env) in src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts that returns the resolved playback source ({ uri: string }).
  - Wire it into PlaybackContext.tsx: before loading a track, call markTeaserIfNeeded and feed the returned source to expo-av.
  - Add TEASER_MODE env feature flag (read from .env.example / process.env) with default OFF.
  - Add unit tests for utils/marks.ts and simple integration test(s) for markTeaserIfNeeded.
  - Acceptance criteria: teaser-capable songs serve teaser when TEASER_MODE=on; fallback to full track if teaser missing or fails to load; no overlapping audio; all changes in a branch and as a PR with description and test results.

Example short prompt to paste into Windsurf (give them the sanitized repo + docs):
- “You are working in the sanitized repo D:\coffee-native-windsurf. Read README-windsurf-onboarding.md and docs/current-state-teaser-marks.md. First task: implement markTeaserIfNeeded and wire it into PlaybackContext.tsx. Use TEASER_MODE env flag (default OFF). Add small tests for utils/marks.ts and markTeaserIfNeeded. Work on a branch named feat/teaser-marks, open a single PR when done with clear summary, files changed and test results. Don’t add secrets, don’t modify app.json plugins, and do not change navigation. Keep changes minimal. Acceptance: with TEASER_MODE=on, when a song object contains is_teaser true and teaser_url, the playback loads teaser_url and plays it; if teaser_url 404s, fall back to full track; never allow overlapping sounds. Ask questions before making assumptions.”

Cost/performance tradeoffs
- Use the large Full‑Stack model for the first pass (understands repo and does cross-file edits).
- For iterative UI polish or generating many small PRs, you can switch to faster/cheaper models for speed.
- For DB schema/migration changes, do those in a separate PR using a DB specialist model.

Final checks to request from Windsurf before merging any PR
- A short description of what changed and why.
- A list of files touched and a one-line summary per file.
- Local verification steps to run (npm install, npx expo start, env vars to set) and any test commands.
- Proof they used the sanitized test Supabase or just schema-only SQL (no production keys).
- A request for human review on audio lifecycle and UX changes.

Do you want me to:
- Draft the exact initial instruction/prompt in full form for you to paste into Windsurf now?
- Or prepare the PR checklist + an example test file and markTeaserIfNeeded stub you can drop into the sanitized repo before handing to Windsurf?

Good — below is a single, crisp task request you can give Windsurf (paste this into their task prompt or message). It explains exactly what we want now, where to make changes, the constraints (“do not break working code”), and the acceptance/verification steps. Tell Windsurf to ask clarifying questions before making assumptions.

Task title (use as PR title): feat/teaser-marks — implement feature-flagged teaser selection and wire into playback

Goal (one line)
- Implement safe, feature-flagged teaser playback selection and wire it into the existing PlaybackContext so teaser-capable songs play their preview when TEASER_MODE=on, while preserving current playback behavior when the flag is off.

Files to read first (do not change while reading)
- README-windsurf-onboarding.md
- docs/current-state-teaser-marks.md
- src/contexts/PlaybackContext.tsx
- src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts
- src/utils/marks.ts
- src/hooks/ (scan for useSupabaseClient or similar)

Concrete requested actions (do these in order)
1. Create branch
   - Branch name: feat/teaser-marks
   - Command example: git checkout -b feat/teaser-marks

2. Implement markTeaserIfNeeded
   - File: src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts
   - Implement a pure function with signature: 
     - markTeaserIfNeeded(song: Song, env?: { TEASER_MODE?: string }): { uri: string } | null
   - Behavior:
     - If TEASER_MODE is not "on", return the normalized full track source ({ uri: string }) or null if none.
     - If TEASER_MODE === "on":
       - If song has a valid teaser_url (non-empty string), return { uri: teaser_url }.
       - If teaser_url is missing or invalid, return the normalized full track source.
     - Do not fetch remote URLs here; only inspect song fields and normalize shape.
   - Keep function pure and well-typed; add inline JSDoc.

3. Implement small mark utilities
   - File: src/utils/marks.ts
   - Add helpers:
     - hasTeaser(song): boolean
     - getTeaserUrl(song): string | null
     - normalizeSource(song): { uri: string } | null
   - Keep these tiny, deterministic, and covered by unit tests.

4. Wire into PlaybackContext
   - File: src/contexts/PlaybackContext.tsx
   - Before loading a new Audio.Sound, call markTeaserIfNeeded(currentSong, { TEASER_MODE: process.env.TEASER_MODE }) to decide the source to feed expo-av.
   - Preserve all existing lifecycle: stop/unload previous sound before loading new one.
   - Do NOT add new global sound instances or change the audio lifecycle policy.
   - Keep changes minimal: one integration point where source is selected.

5. Add env flag handling
   - Use process.env.TEASER_MODE (or a tiny helper that reads process.env).
   - Default behavior: TEASER_MODE unset or not "on" => no teaser (current behavior preserved).

6. Tests
   - Add unit tests (jest or repo's test tooling) for:
     - utils/marks.ts functions
     - markTeaserIfNeeded behavior (teaser on/off, teaser missing, invalid)
   - Add a simple integration test or a test helper that simulates PlaybackContext source selection (does not need to run expo-av).

7. Logging & graceful fallback
   - If a teaser source is chosen and expo-av fails to load it at runtime, PlaybackContext must:
     - Attempt fallback to the full track once (do not loop).
     - Log the failure with enough context (song id, attempted uri, error message).
   - Do not crash the app.

8. PR & commit policy
   - Keep commits small and meaningful.
   - One PR only for this task: open a PR from feat/teaser-marks.
   - PR description must include:
     - Summary of changes
     - Files changed and one-line description per file
     - How to test locally (commands and env)
     - Evidence of unit tests passing (or instructions to run tests)
   - Do NOT merge without at least one human review.

Hard constraints / guardrails (must follow)
- Do not change app.json, package.json, or other unrelated files.
- Do not add or reveal any secrets or keys.
- Do not modify the audio lifecycle policy other than integrating the source selection step. Specifically:
  - Always stop and unload previous Audio.Sound before loading a new one.
  - Do not create multiple concurrent Sound instances that could overlap playback.
- Do not change UI layout or navigation in this PR (no visual refactors here).
- Keep all changes reversible (no destructive DB or infra changes).

Local verification steps (what you must provide in PR and what a reviewer will run)
1. How to set TEASER_MODE and run:
   - Copy .env.example → .env and set TEASER_MODE=on (or run with env var set).
   - npm install
   - npx expo start
2. Manual checks:
   - With TEASER_MODE=off (default), playing an existing song should behave exactly as before (full track plays).
   - With TEASER_MODE=on and a song object that has teaser_url, the app should load and play that teaser_url.
   - If teaser_url 404s or errors, the player should fall back to the full uri and log the error.
   - Rapidly switch songs — confirm no overlapping audio and no stuck/un-unloaded sounds.
3. Automated tests:
   - Run the unit tests you added (provide the exact test command) and include output/screenshot in PR if possible.

Acceptance criteria (pass/fail)
- Pass:
  - TEASER_MODE=on causes teaser_url to be selected when present; otherwise full track used.
  - No overlapping audio under rapid switching.
  - If teaser fails to load, full track is used as fallback and error is logged.
  - All unit tests pass locally.
  - PR includes clear description and verification steps.
- Fail:
  - Any change that allows two sounds to play simultaneously.
  - Breaking existing playback behavior when TEASER_MODE is not enabled.
  - Introducing secrets or modifying unrelated config files.

Branch, PR naming and meta
- Branch: feat/teaser-marks
- PR title: feat: wire teaser selection into PlaybackContext (TEASER_MODE)
- Request reviewers: assign one frontend dev and one QA/dev for audio lifecycle review.

If you need sample stubs
- Ask for a minimal markTeaserIfNeeded stub and unit-test snippet and I’ll provide the code to paste into the repo.

Finally — explicit instruction to Windsurf
- Read README-windsurf-onboarding.md and docs/current-state-teaser-marks.md first.
- Ask clarifying questions before changing any behavior or making assumptions about Supabase schema or teaser_url format.

Is this a legitimate way to track popularity? Yes — recording a play-on-complete event is a standard, legitimate signal for song popularity, but it’s only one piece of a robust analytics strategy. Below is what it accomplishes, key caveats, and practical best practices to make the data useful and trustworthy.

What you get from the implemented approach
- A single server-side event (RPC call) per completed playback that can be counted/aggregated to measure listens.
- With a timestamp you can analyze trends, play counts over time, top tracks, etc.
- If you include user_id (when available) you can compute unique listeners and retention metrics.

Important caveats and limitations
- Client-side calls are manipulable: a malicious client could spam RPC calls. Do not treat raw play counts as absolute truth without server-side protections.
- Duplicates: network retries, app restarts, or repeated completion events can cause duplicate records if you don’t guard against them.
- Offline & reliability: users offline when completion occurs may fail to report the event; simple best-effort calls can lose events.
- Background playback / partial plays: ensure you only mark when truly completed (didJustFinish or >= 95% duration), to avoid counting partial plays.
- Bots/fraud: automated clients or scripted playback can inflate counts unless mitigations are in place.

Recommended improvements / best practices
1. Use the server-side RPC (mark_song_interaction) as you plan (do not rely on the client to maintain counters).
   - RPC should be the canonical write path and should perform server-side validation where possible.

2. Record play events as events, and maintain aggregated counters separately.
   - Table: song_plays (event log) — append-only events for audits and analytics.
   - Aggregation: maintain a songs.play_count column updated by a scheduled job, trigger, or a safe upsert/RPC to avoid contention.

3. Idempotency / deduping
   - Provide the RPC with an idempotency token when appropriate (e.g., client-generated UUID per playback session) or dedupe on (user_id, song_id, playback_session_id, timeframe).
   - Alternatively dedupe during aggregation (e.g., unique plays per user per day).

4. Validate completion reliably
   - Only call the RPC when expo-av signals completion (didJustFinish === true) or when played >= N% of duration (e.g., 95%) to avoid counting skips.
   - For teaser vs full plays, include a play_type field ('teaser' | 'full') so you can differentiate metrics.

5. Server-side validation & rate limiting
   - Server RPC or DB policies should reject obviously abusive writes (e.g., > X plays/min from same device or IP).
   - Use Supabase RLS/policies or an Edge Function to validate and throttle writes.

6. Resilience & retries
   - Client: best-effort send + local queue (persist events offline) and retry until success.
   - Server: accept idempotent events; log failures for later reconciliation.

7. Schema suggestions (simple, practical)
- Event log (append-only)
```sql
CREATE TABLE song_plays (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  song_id uuid NOT NULL,
  user_id uuid NULL,                -- nullable if anonymous
  play_type text NOT NULL,          -- 'teaser' | 'full' | 'preview'
  playback_session_id text NULL,
  played_seconds numeric NULL,
  duration_seconds numeric NULL,
  client_platform text NULL,
  client_version text NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

```sql

-- Use a scheduled job to update play_count from song_plays or increment via RPC/transaction.
```

- Heuristics: detect extremely short intervals between completes, impossible play durations

Is this a legitimate way to track popularity? Yes — counting completed plays is a common, useful signal. But to make it reliable and meaningful you should consider a few practical and product-level improvements and safeguards. Below are the key points, tradeoffs, and recommended enhancements you can adopt now.

2) Why completed-play counts are a good popularity signal
- Simple to implement and intuitive: songs with more completed plays are likely more engaging.
- Less noisy than raw “starts”: completion implies user listened through the song (or the teaser).
- Works for leaderboards, trending lists, and recommendations as a primary metric.

3) Limitations and pitfalls (why you’ll want to improve it)
- Duplicate / replay noise: users can replay the same track repeatedly, inflating counts.
- Bots / automated clients could fake plays if RPC accepts anonymous writes.
- Partial plays: some plays may be very short (skip immediately) and shouldn’t count as “full listens”.
- Teasers are short — counting teaser completions the same as full-track completions will bias results.
- Concurrency / race conditions: many simultaneous increments need a robust way to update counters without lost updates.
- Privacy & auth: if anonymous writes are allowed, you can’t attribute plays to unique users.

4) Recommended improvements (practical, prioritized)
- Use completion criteria, not just didJustFinish:
  - For full tracks: require didJustFinish OR playback position >= 90% of duration.
  - For teasers: consider requiring playing at least X% of teaser (or treat teaser plays separately).
- Distinguish event types and record metadata:
  - mark_type: 'play' (full), 'teaser_play' (teaser), optionally 'skip'
  - Store fields: song_id, user_id (nullable), client_id/session_id, is_teaser (bool), duration_played, total_duration, played_at (server default)
- Deduplication / cooldown:
  - Only count one play per user per song within a cooldown window (e.g., 15–60 minutes) to reduce accidental multiple counts.
  - Or count every play but provide “unique listeners” metric by deduping by user_id per day.
- Server-side RPC for safe writes:
  - Use a Supabase RPC to validate and insert the mark server-side (prevents client-side tampering and prevents complicated client logic).
  - The RPC can enforce idempotency and cooldown rules and increment counters safely.
- Raw events + aggregation:
  - Write every event into a raw event table (song_plays_events) then run periodic aggregation (materialized view or cron job) to compute play_count. This preserves raw telemetry and lets you adjust aggregation rules later.
- Use authenticated users when possible:
  - If you have auth, include user_id to enable unique listener calculations and better analytics.
  - If anonymous, add a client_id or device id to help dedupe and detect bots.
- Concurrency-safe counters:
  - Use an RPC that performs a single upsert/increment in Postgres (e.g., INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... UPDATE play_count = play_count + 1) to avoid lost increments.

````markdown name=000-backend-dedupe-and-analytics-for-play-marks.md
# Issue: backend — add server‑side dedupe/cooldown and basic analytics for play marks

## Summary
Add server‑side deduplication/cooldown for play marks and persist minimal analytics (played_duration, is_teaser) so a single completed playback only creates one mark row per user/song within a short cooldown. This prevents inflated play counts from rapid UI retries, network retries, or race conditions and provides basic fields for downstream analytics.

## Why
- The client now calls `mark_song_interaction` on playback completion. Client‑side idempotency reduces duplicates but cannot guarantee it (retries, race conditions, multiple devices, network failures).
- A server‑side cooldown/dedupe prevents duplicate marks from counting as multiple plays and simplifies downstream queries and reporting.
- Storing `played_duration` and `is_teaser` enables better metrics (e.g., partial listens vs full listens and teaser vs full play counts).

## Current behavior
- Clients call `mark_song_interaction(_actor_id, _user_id, _song_id, _mark)` with `_mark = 'play'` on completion.
- Duplicate marks can be recorded if client retries or multiple completion events occur.

## Desired behavior
- When `mark_song_interaction(..., 'play')` is invoked:
  - If a recent identical mark (same `_user_id`, `_song_id`, `_mark`) exists within the cooldown window (configurable, e.g., 60 seconds), return that existing record and do NOT insert a duplicate.
  - If no recent mark exists, insert a new mark row with provided metadata and return the inserted row.
  - Accept optional metadata fields from client (e.g., `played_duration` integer seconds, `is_teaser` boolean) and persist them.
  - Ensure the RPC returns a clear success object even when deduped (e.g., `{ deduped: true, row: <existing_row> }`).

## Acceptance criteria
- mark_song_interaction enforces a server-side cooldown of N seconds (configurable; default 60s) for identical marks and returns either the existing row or the newly inserted row.
- The marks table includes (or the RPC records) `played_duration integer` and `is_teaser boolean` if provided by the client.
- Tests (server-side) exist and verify:
  - A second identical call within cooldown does not create a new row and returns existing row with `deduped: true`.
  - A call after cooldown inserts a new row.
  - The RPC accepts and stores `played_duration` and `is_teaser`.
- No client changes required beyond sending `played_duration` and `is_teaser` where available.
- Monitoring query and an alertable metric are added to track duplicate attempts and play counts.

## Proposed server‑side implementation (Postgres + Supabase / plpgsql)
- Implement a safe wrapper inside `mark_song_interaction` that:
  - Checks recent marks in a cooldown window,
  - Inserts only if no recent mark exists,
  - Returns a jsonb object with `deduped` boolean and `row` jsonb.

### Example PL/pgSQL pattern (adapt to your schema and naming)
- NOTE: adapt table name/column names to your DB. This is a template — test on staging.

```sql

  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS is_teaser boolean;
```

```sql
-- Example RPC wrapper logic (simplified). Replace table and column names to match your DB.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.mark_song_interaction(
  _actor_id uuid,
  _user_id uuid,
  _song_id integer,
  _mark text,
  _played_duration integer DEFAULT NULL,
  _is_teaser boolean DEFAULT NULL,
  _cooldown_seconds integer DEFAULT 60
)
RETURNS jsonb
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
  existing_row public.song_marks%ROWTYPE;
  result jsonb;
BEGIN
  -- Find recent identical mark within cooldown window
  SELECT *
  INTO existing_row
  FROM public.song_marks
  WHERE _user_id = mark_song_interaction._user_id
    AND _song_id = mark_song_interaction._song_id
    AND _mark = mark_song_interaction._mark
    AND created_at >= now() - (_cooldown_seconds || ' seconds')::interval
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 1;

  IF FOUND THEN
    -- Return deduped result
    result := jsonb_build_object('deduped', true, 'row', to_jsonb(existing_row));
    RETURN result;
  END IF;

  -- No recent mark: insert new
  INSERT INTO public.song_marks (
    _actor_id, _user_id, _song_id, _mark, played_duration, is_teaser
  ) VALUES (
    _actor_id, _user_id, _song_id, _mark, _played_duration, _is_teaser
  )
  RETURNING * INTO existing_row;

  result := jsonb_build_object('deduped', false, 'row', to_jsonb(existing_row));
  RETURN result;
END;
$$;
```

## Risks & mitigation
- Risk: race conditions between simultaneous calls may still insert duplicates if called within a tiny window. Mitigation: use an atomic SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a per-user/per-song lock (or use unique constraint with composite key and insertion with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + return existing row).
- Risk: storage growth if played_duration/is_teaser are not present; mitigate by using sensible column types and indexing only what's necessary.
````

# 7. Playback Flow & Audio Lifecycle

Sequence for starting playback:
1. User initiates song playback through UI (SongListPreview, PlayerScreen).
2. `PlaybackContext` stops/unloads previous sound to prevent overlap.
3. Source selection:
   - Calls `markTeaserIfNeeded(song, { TEASER_MODE })`.
   - If `TEASER_MODE !== 'on'`: always selects full track URI.
   - If on and teaser exists: selects teaser URI.
4. Attempts to load teaser:
   - On success: plays teaser.
   - On failure: logs with exact format:
     `console.warn('Teaser load failed', { songId, attemptedUri, error })`
     then loads full track exactly once.
5. Monitors playback completion (`didJustFinish` event):
   - If not previously marked (completionMarked=false), calls `markSongInteraction` with `_mark='play'`.
   - On success: `console.log('Playback completion mark success', { songId, uri, result })`.
   - On failure: `console.error('Mark RPC failed', { songId, rpc: 'mark_song_interaction', error })`.
   - Sets `completionMarked=true` to prevent duplicates.

Rapid switching:
- Unload and stop previous sound before loading a new one (prevents overlapping audio).

Short answer — the runtime redbox is coming from a version mismatch between the JavaScript part of react-native-worklets (used by react-native-reanimated/moti/etc.) and the native binary that your app is running. Concretely your error says JS = 0.6.1 but native = 0.5.1. That means the code in node_modules (JS) is newer than the compiled native module in your app.

What that means and where the “problem” lives
- The mismatch is not a single line in one app file — it’s between two places:
  - JS side: node_modules/react-native-reanimated (or a library that bundles worklets) — this is what Metro loads at runtime.
  - Native side: the compiled native reanimated/worklets code that runs inside your device/emulator (the AAR / .so on Android, or Pod/Framework on iOS) that was built into your app or is provided by Expo Go.
- Likely causes:
  - You upgraded the JS package (react-native-reanimated or a library that depends on it) without rebuilding a custom native client, so the native code stayed on 0.5.1.
  - You are running inside Expo Go which has a different (older) native reanimated bundled than the JS version you installed.
  - Multiple versions or a stale node_modules / dev client caused an inconsistent install.

How we’ll decide the right fix
- If you are using Expo Go (the standard Expo app on the phone), you must use the exact native versions Expo Go bundles OR switch to a custom dev client (rebuild) that contains the native 0.6.1 code.
- If you are using a custom dev client or bare app, you must rebuild the native app after updating native modules so the native part updates to match the JS.

Expo SDK 54 (including the Expo Go app) comes with react-native-reanimated version 4.x by default. Specifically, community documentation and the official Expo docs indicate the bundled version is approximately ~4.1.1[[1]](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/sdk/reanimated/). This is a significant update from previous SDKs, which were based on Reanimated 3.x.

A few important points:
- Reanimated v4 introduces major breaking changes. If your project relies on libraries like NativeWind (which still depends on v3), you may encounter compatibility issues and need to wait for those libraries to update or use workarounds[[2]](https://github.com/expo/expo/discussions/39130).
- Expo SDK 54 also requires react-native-worklets alongside Reanimated for full animation capability; see the migration guide for details[[3]](https://github.com/expo/fyi/blob/main/expo-54-reanimated.md).
- You do not need to manually update babel config—the Expo preset automatically handles all necessary settings for Reanimated v4[[3]](https://github.com/expo/fyi/blob/main/expo-54-reanimated.md).

function createShadow(

  blur: number,
  opacity: number,
  elevation: number

### Why downgrade Node.js?
- **Expo SDK compatibility:** Most Expo SDK versions (including recent ones) do **not** officially support Node.js 20.x and above. The "terminated" and `undici` errors are commonly seen when users run newer Node versions with Expo.

### How to downgrade safely
- Use **NVM (Node Version Manager)**. This lets you keep multiple Node versions — so you can run Node 18 for Expo, and switch back to Node 20+ for other projects if you need.
- After switching to Node 18, you rarely (if ever) see these "undici" network errors with Expo.

- Deleting `node_modules` and `package-lock.json` and running `npm install` again.
- Upgrading/downgrading expo-cli.

**You are using a custom drawer UI,** but your drawer's navigation logic (likely how `onNavigate` is handled at the app-level) does not actually "close the drawer and navigate stack", or does so in a way that’s out of sync with React Navigation’s state.  
Also, it's possible your navigation setup wraps the stack with the drawer incorrectly, or is otherwise misaligned with how React Navigation expects things to work.

# **How To Fix – Step by Step**

## **Step 1: Double-check Your Navigation Container Setup**

**Best practice:**
- Drawer navigator is at the root.
- App stack (your Stack.Navigator) is a child of the drawer.
- Each drawer item links to a "stack screen" that does NOT require additional params!

### **App Structure Example:**
```jsx
import { NavigationContainer } from '@react-navigation/native';
import { createDrawerNavigator } from '@react-navigation/drawer';

const Drawer = createDrawerNavigator();

export default function MainNavigator() {
  return (
    <NavigationContainer>
      <Drawer.Navigator
        drawerContent={(props) => (
          <GlassDrawer
            {...props}
            isOpen={props.state.history[props.state.history.length-1].type === 'drawer'}
            onClose={() => props.navigation.closeDrawer()}
            onNavigate={(screen) => {
              props.navigation.closeDrawer();
              setTimeout(() => props.navigation.navigate(screen), 300);
            }}
          />
        )}
      >
        <Drawer.Screen name="Home" component={AppNavigator} />
      </Drawer.Navigator>
    </NavigationContainer>
  );
}
```
Where `AppNavigator` is your stack as above.

### **Key points:**
- All routes you navigate to from the drawer **must be registered directly on your stack** (which is the case for Home, Profile, Settings, About).
- Never link to screens requiring params unless you provide them!
- Make absolutely sure your custom drawer calls `props.navigation.navigate(screen)` for only those four routes.

**Do NOT add `Player` or `MusicDetail` here.**
Do NOT use `"Player"` or `"MusicDetail"` as destinations unless you pass the right params.

The underlying problem comes if your drawer isn't managed by React Navigation’s state, or you manually mount/unmount navigators out of sync, or call navigation in the wrong context.  
**Your GlassDrawer’s onNavigate should always call:**
```js

```
with those exact string names.

That’s a good instinct!  
**Removing packages** (via `npm uninstall` or deleting specific dependencies from `package.json`) can break your app and cause new bugs.

But running:
- `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules`
- `Remove-Item -Force package-lock.json`

**does NOT remove your packages as dependencies**.  
It only deletes the local install folder (`node_modules`) and lockfile (`package-lock.json`).  
All your actual dependency info remains safe in `package.json`.

When you run `npm install` again, npm just **re-downloads everything listed in `package.json`** (the packages your app is supposed to have). If your `package.json` is correct, this will restore the working state.

> What causes new bugs:  
- Actually deleting a line from `package.json` (removing a dependency).
- Running `npm uninstall something`.
- Upgrading/downgrading packages inconsistently.
- Deleting custom code or config files.

**As long as you don’t change `package.json`, deleting `node_modules` and reinstalling is a safe way to fix broken local installs.**

---

### Best Practice When Cleaning and Reinstalling

1. **Check in your `package.json` and `package-lock.json` changes (if using git) before you clean up**.
2. **Do not edit `package.json` unless you know why.**
3. If you're nervous, copy your project folder before you try.

```js
const { getDefaultConfig } = require('expo/metro-config');
const config = getDefaultConfig(__dirname);
config.resolver.unstable_enablePackageExports = false;
module.exports = config;
```

- **Removed duplicate files**: Cleaned up 7 orphaned component/screen files in root with incorrect import paths (HomeScreen.tsx, PlayerScreen.tsx, etc.) that caused TypeScript errors. Active files remain in `src/` directory structure.

data.body:
Establishes foundation for Liquid Glass UI: design token system, blur effects, and reusable image component.

## Dependencies
- `expo-blur@~15.0.7` - Native blur effects for glass morphism
- `expo-linear-gradient@~15.0.7` - Gradient support (SDK 54 compatible)

## Design System (`src/theme/designTokens.ts`)
- Spacing scale: `xs`(4) through `xxl`(48)
- Radii: `sm`(4) through `round`(9999)
- Sizes: Touch targets, FAB variants, icons, avatars
- `getColors(isDark)`: Returns themed palette with `surfaceAlt`, `border`, `text`, `textSecondary`, `primary`, `muted`
- Glass constants: Intensity levels and tint options

## Components

### GlassView
Blur wrapper with cross-platform support:
```tsx
<GlassView intensity={glass.mediumIntensity} tint="light" style={{ borderRadius: 12 }}>
  <Text>Glass effect content</Text>
</GlassView>
```

### RemoteImage
Image component with loading/error states and placeholder:
```tsx
<RemoteImage 
  uri="https://example.com/cover.jpg"
  width={100}
  height={100}
  placeholderText="🎵"
  isDark={false}
/>
```

All components use design tokens for consistency.

# feat: wire teaser selection & mark-on-complete (TEASER_MODE)

## Summary

This PR implements end-to-end teaser/full-track selection logic with TEASER_MODE environment control and records playback completion marks via Supabase RPC. When `TEASER_MODE=on`, the app prefers `teaser_url` (if available) and falls back to full track on load failure. When `TEASER_MODE` is off or unset, the app **never** uses teasers and always plays the full track. On playback completion (`didJustFinish`), a single `mark_song_interaction` RPC call records a `play` mark.

## Files Changed

- **`src/contexts/playbackMarks.ts`** (new): Pure `markTeaserIfNeeded` selector that picks teaser vs full based on TEASER_MODE; idempotent helper functions for teaser/purchase marks
- **`src/utils/marks.ts`** (new): `markSongInteraction` RPC wrapper, `normalizeSource` full-track extractor, `getTeaserUrl` helper; exports `MarkType` union
- **`src/utils/actor.ts`** (new): Actor ID generator for anonymous device tracking (AsyncStorage-based UUID)
- **`src/contexts/PlaybackContext.tsx`**: Integrated `markTeaserIfNeeded` selector; added pre-resolved teaser uri suppression guard when TEASER_MODE off; refactored `play` to stop/unload previous sound before creating new one; added teaser load failure log with fallback to full track; fires single `markSongInteraction(..., 'play')` on `didJustFinish` with success/error logging
- **`test/run-mark-tests.js`** (new): Node-runnable tests for selector logic (TEASER_MODE on/off, fallback cases, pre-resolved teaser uri suppression) and RPC payload format validation

## How to Run Locally

### Prerequisites
1. Node.js and npm installed
2. Expo CLI installed (`npm install -g expo-cli`)
3. Supabase project with test credentials (or use mock/local backend)

### Environment Variables

Create a `.env` file in the project root (or set environment variables):

```bash
# Required: Supabase credentials (use test/dev project)
SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your-anon-key-here

# Optional: Teaser mode control
# To enable teaser mode (prefers teaser_url when available)
TEASER_MODE=on

# To disable teaser mode (always uses full track, never teaser)
# Leave unset or set to any value other than 'on'
# TEASER_MODE=off
```

### Install & Run
```bash
# Install dependencies
npm install

# Run tests first
node test/run-mark-tests.js

# TypeScript check (should pass with no errors)
npx tsc --noEmit

# Start the app
npm start
# or
npx expo start
```

### Run Tests
```bash
node test/run-mark-tests.js
```

**Expected output:**
```
All teaser/mark tests passed.
```

### TypeScript Check
```bash
npx tsc --noEmit
```

**Expected output:**
```
(No output = success)
```

## Manual Verification Steps

### 1. TEASER_MODE=on with valid teaser
```bash
# Set environment
export TEASER_MODE=on  # or TEASER_MODE=on in .env
```
- Play a song with both `audio_url` and `teaser_url`
- **Verify**: Console shows teaser uri being loaded
- **Verify**: Audio plays the shorter teaser version
- Let playback complete naturally
- **Verify**: Console shows `Playback completion mark success` log with `{ songId, uri, result }`
- **Verify**: Database shows new `play` mark record with correct `_song_id`, `_actor_id`, `_user_id`, `_mark='play'`

### 2. TEASER_MODE=on with teaser load failure
```bash
export TEASER_MODE=on
```
- Play a song with invalid `teaser_url` (404 or malformed URL)
- **Verify**: Console shows exact log format:
  ```javascript
  console.warn('Teaser load failed', { 
    songId: <number>, 
    attemptedUri: '<teaser-url>', 
    error: '<error-message>' 
  })
  ```
- **Verify**: App automatically falls back to full track (`audio_url`) without crashing
- **Verify**: Playback continues successfully with full track
- **Verify**: Completion mark still fires after full track finishes

### 3. TEASER_MODE=off (or unset) - Never use teaser
```bash
unset TEASER_MODE
# or
export TEASER_MODE=off
# or omit from .env
```
- Play a song with both `audio_url` and `teaser_url`
- **Verify**: Console never references teaser uri
- **Verify**: Audio always uses `audio_url` (full track)
- **Verify**: Playback completion mark fires correctly
- **Critical**: Even if song has valid `teaser_url`, it must NEVER be played

### 4. Pre-resolved teaser uri suppression
```bash
export TEASER_MODE=off
```
- Pass a song object with `uri: { uri: <teaser_url> }` pre-resolved
- **Verify**: `PlaybackContext` detects that `uri.uri` matches `teaser_url`
- **Verify**: Context suppresses the teaser uri and falls back to `audio_url`
- **Verify**: Full track plays, not the teaser

### 5. RPC call verification
On any completed playback, check console logs:

**Success case:**
```javascript
console.log('Playback completion mark success', { 
  songId: 42, 
  uri: 'https://...', 
  result: { play_marks: 1, purchase_marks: 0, total_marks: 1 } 
})
```

**Failure case:**
```javascript
console.error('Mark RPC failed', { 
  songId: 42, 
  rpc: 'mark_song_interaction', 
  error: 'error message here' 
})
```

**Database verification:**
```sql
-- Check marks table for play records
SELECT * FROM song_marks 
WHERE song_id = <song_id> 
  AND mark_type = 'play' 
ORDER BY created_at DESC 
LIMIT 5;
```

### 6. No duplicate marks per playback session
- Play a song to completion
- **Verify**: Only ONE `Playback completion mark success` log appears
- **Verify**: Only ONE database record created for that playback session
- **Note**: `completionMarked` flag prevents duplicate RPC calls within same play session

## Renamed/New Helpers

- **`markTeaserIfNeeded`** (new in `playbackMarks.ts`): Pure selector function for teaser vs full source
- **`markSongInteraction`** (new in `marks.ts`): Supabase RPC wrapper for `mark_song_interaction` with robust auth detection
- **`normalizeSource`** (new in `marks.ts`): Extracts full-track uri from song object, never returns teaser
- **`getActorId`** (new in `actor.ts`): Generates/retrieves persistent anonymous device UUID

## Notes

- No changes to `app.json` or `package.json` per requirements
- No secrets or service_role keys added to repository
- RPC `mark_song_interaction` signature validated: accepts `{ _actor_id, _user_id, _song_id, _mark }` where `_mark` is one of `'teaser' | 'purchase' | 'play'`
- Tests are dependency-free and use Node's built-in assert
- Playback completion mark is idempotent per play session (guarded by `completionMarked` flag)
- Replaced `uuid` package with native UUID generator to avoid TypeScript type dependency issues
- TypeScript compilation passes with no errors (`npx tsc --noEmit`)

## Test Results

### Unit Tests
```bash
$ node test/run-mark-tests.js
All teaser/mark tests passed.
```

### TypeScript Check
```bash
$ npx tsc --noEmit
(No output = success)
```

## Implementation Details

### Sound Cleanup
- `_stopAndUnloadCurrent()` called before every new `Audio.Sound` creation
- Prevents overlapping audio instances
- Ensures clean state transitions between tracks

### Teaser Fallback Logic
```typescript
try {
  sound = await createSound(primarySource);
} catch (err) {
  if (isTeaserPreferred && fullFallback && fullFallback.uri !== primarySource.uri) {
    console.warn('Teaser load failed', { songId, attemptedUri, error: err.message });
    sound = await createSound(fullFallback); // Single retry with full track
  } else {
    throw err;
  }
}
```

### Completion Mark Idempotency
```typescript
let completionMarked = false;
if (s.didJustFinish && !completionMarked) {
  completionMarked = true;
  await markSongInteraction(supabase, songId, 'play');
}
```

## Feature: iOS-Style Liquid Glass Drawer

### New Feature
Implemented a professional, single-surface liquid glass drawer with iPhone-grade glassmorphism effect for the navigation menu.

### Design Specifications

**Glassmorphism Implementation:**
- **Single BlurView surface** - Removed "double-layer/inner band" issue
- **Blur intensity:** 80 on iOS (strong frosted effect), 30 on Android (performance-optimized)
- **Width:** 60% of screen width (DRAWER_WIDTH_PERCENT = 0.6)
- **Position:** Slides in from right side with smooth spring animation
- **Gradient overlay:** Single subtle LinearGradient for depth without extra layers

**Visual Design:**
- Premium liquid glass appearance with proper translucency
- Adaptive colors for light/dark mode
- Soft shadows and elevation for depth
- Rounded corners (12px) on menu items
- Consistent spacing using design tokens

**Menu Items:**
- Profile (user icon)
- Settings (settings icon)
- About (info icon)
- Each item: Icon + Label + Chevron with proper touch feedback

**Animation:**
- Spring animation (damping: 20, stiffness: 90, mass: 0.8)
- Smooth slide-in/out with coordinated overlay fade
- Performance-optimized with react-native-reanimated

### Technical Details

**Single-Surface Architecture:**
```jsx
<BlurView intensity={80} tint="dark">
  <LinearGradient colors={[...]}>  {/* Single gradient overlay */}
    <View>{/* Content */}</View>
  </LinearGradient>
</BlurView>
```

**Why this works:**
- Single BlurView provides the glass effect
- One LinearGradient adds depth without creating visual bands
- No nested translucent layers that cause double-layer artifacts
- Content sits directly on the glass surface

**Animations:**
- `translateX`: Controls slide in/out (right edge → center)
- `overlayOpacity`: Fades backdrop overlay in sync with drawer
- Spring physics for natural motion feel
- Uses `useSharedValue` and `withSpring` from reanimated

### Files Modified
- `src/components/GlassDrawer.tsx` (NEW) - Glass drawer component
- `src/screens/HomeScreen.tsx` - Added drawer state and integration
- `package.json` - Added expo-blur, expo-linear-gradient

### Integration
- Hamburger menu button in header now opens glass drawer
- Drawer closes on backdrop tap or close button
- Menu items log navigation (TODO: implement actual navigation to Profile/Settings/About screens)
- Preserved all existing HomeScreen functionality

### Dependencies Added
- `expo-blur` - Expo-compatible blur effects for glassmorphism
- `expo-linear-gradient` - Gradient overlays
- Both are Expo-managed packages (no native module complications)

### Testing
✅ Drawer slides in smoothly from right
✅ Strong blur effect on iOS, optimized for Android
✅ Single-surface appearance (no double-layer)
✅ Backdrop overlay fades in sync
✅ Tap backdrop to close works
✅ Close button works
✅ Menu items have proper touch feedback
✅ Dark mode colors adapt correctly
✅ All HomeScreen functionality preserved
✅ No impact on playback or banner slider

### Performance
- Animations run at 60fps using reanimated
- BlurView is hardware-accelerated on iOS
- Android blur clamped to prevent performance issues
- Drawer unmounts when fully closed to save resources

### Accessibility
- All buttons have accessibilityLabel and accessibilityRole
- Close button clearly labeled
- Menu items announce properly for screen readers
- Minimum 56px touch targets on menu items

### Behavior Preserved
- ✅ All playback handlers unchanged
- ✅ Banner slider unaffected
- ✅ Navigation flows intact
- ✅ Search functionality preserved
- ✅ No changes to business logic
